foodDescription: Egg whites, sugar, and a little flour baked into three golden peaks, for the city’s three hills, and dusted with sugar. Made to order for two and eaten at once.

A ball of pistachio marzipan and nougat dipped in dark chocolate, invented by confectioner Paul Fürst in 1890. The Fürst shops still make them by hand. The factory-made red-and-gold ones are a different product.
Grilled bratwurst in a toasted roll with onions, mustard, and curry powder. Said to have been invented in 1949 by a Bulgarian cook at the Balkan Grill on Getreidegasse, which still sells only this.
Small flour dumplings tossed in a pan with strong mountain cheese and topped with fried onions. Hearty Alpine food from the Pinzgau valleys south of the city, often served in the pan.
A thin veal cutlet in a crisp, puffy crust, served with lemon and potato salad. Only veal may be called Wiener Schnitzel; the pork version is “Schnitzel vom Schwein.”
A thick, fluffy pancake torn into pieces in the pan, dusted with sugar, and served with plum compote or applesauce. Big enough to be a meal.
A large steamed dumpling filled with plum jam, covered in melted butter and poppy seeds with sugar. A favorite at mountain huts and ski lodges.
A wooden board of cured meats, bacon, cheese, spreads, pickles, and dark bread, eaten with beer or wine in the afternoon or evening.
A dense, dark Christmas loaf packed with dried pears, figs, prunes, and nuts. Sold at the Christmas markets and sliced thin with butter.
Salzburg’s big brewery, founded in 1492 and still owned by a local family. Its beer is poured almost everywhere in the city, and the brewery has a museum.
A lager brewed at Mülln since 1621 and served only from wooden barrels, in the brewery’s own beer hall and garden. Not the same brewery as Munich’s Augustiner.
Hot spiced red wine sold at the Christmas markets from late November, in mugs you return for a deposit or keep. Punsch is the stronger, fruitier cousin.
